lesson_title: The Gas Braai Equation: Balancing in Four Moves
hook_text: Every time a gas braai lights, five oxygen molecules meet one propane molecule. Here is how we know.
clip_script: Light a gas braai and propane, C3H8, burns in oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water. But how much oxygen does each propane molecule need? Balance the equation and find out. Rule one: atoms are never made or destroyed, so every atom on the left must turn up on the right. Rule two: only change the big numbers in front, never the little numbers inside. Now count. Three carbons on the left, so three carbon dioxides on the right. Eight hydrogens on the left, so four waters, because four times two is eight. Now the oxygens on the right: six in the carbon dioxide plus four in the water, ten. Ten oxygen atoms means five oxygen molecules. C3H8 plus 5O2 gives 3CO2 plus 4H2O. One propane needs five oxygens, which is why a braai needs plenty of air to burn cleanly. Carbon first, hydrogen next, oxygen last, then check.
visual_style: A gas braai flame zooming into molecules; atoms coloured black, white and red; counters ticking on each side of a big arrow; coefficients dropping into place with a click.
pacing: Quick hook at the braai, steady counting with a beat on each coefficient, a firm finish on the rule.
